offered_action_specs.name: rollback_deploy
offered_action_specs.description: Roll one service back to the settings it ran before its latest deploy, as the deploy log records them. Code plans it from that log, not from your tools' results, so you can name it even when they cannot see deploys: if the log holds no deploy of that service to undo, or the service changed since, code refuses it. Its container is recreated, so the service pauses while it restarts. Money already booked wrong stays wrong: a rollback stops new damage, and repairs nothing.

proposed.why: The evidence chain is complete: provider timeouts and 500s, then retries, then the breaker opens, then fast 503s. No deploy of ours is implicated.

diagnosis.hypothesis: The payment provider (fake-provider, an outside company) degraded starting around 20:51. Some POST /v1/payments calls got 500s, and others hung until payments-api's 3 s read timeout. payments-api tries each charge up to 3 times, so a request whose attempts all time out takes about 9.6 s. That produced the high p95 latency, and these requests ended in 503. Around 20:52 the failures tripped the PROVIDER_BREAKER circuit breaker. Since then payments-api fails POST /payments immediately with 503 ('circuit breaker is open'), leaving payments pending. That is the roughly 8.5/s of 503s, about 90% of answers. The cause is upstream of us. No change on our side explains it: every container was created together at 20:50:33 with the usual settings. The provider-side cause and whether it has recovered are not confirmed. Our client-latency histogram (c5) shows about 5 ms because it apparently records only calls that completed, not the timed-out ones.

evidence.shows: payments-api 503s rise from 0.04/s at 20:51:20 to 8.48/s at 20:52:50, while 201s fall to 0.2/s. This confirms the alert.
Every recent ERROR reads 'provider unavailable; payment left pending: /v1/payments not sent: the circuit breaker is open'.
Provider calls returning 500 grow from 0.05/s to 0.5/s between 20:51:00 and 20:52:12. By 20:52:57 all provider calls stop, which is consistent with the open breaker.
POST /payments traces from 20:52:00 to 20:52:06 take 6.2 to 9.6 s.

A 9.6 s POST /payments made three POSTs to fake-provider /v1/payments. Each ended in httpx ReadTimeout after about 3.0 s, and the request then returned 503. Redis and Postgres calls took under 1.2 ms.
All services, the provider included, were created at 20:50:33 with expected settings (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents). No single deploy of ours stands out as a cause.
The p95 of recorded provider-client calls stays around 5 ms, so the timed-out calls do not appear in this histogram. Latency has to be judged from the traces.

proposed_fix.summary: No rollback fits, because the fault is at the provider and the breaker is doing its job by failing fast. Escalate to the provider and check its status. Watch the breaker's trial calls and close it once the provider answers normally. After recovery, reconcile the payments left pending: resubmit them under the same idempotency keys or let the provider's webhooks confirm them, then run money_check. Separately, consider shortening the 3 s timeout × 3 retries so that requests fail faster while the breaker is still closed.

diagnosis.blast_radius: Taking no action means new payments keep failing with 503 and pending payments stay pending until the provider recovers. Resubmitting pending payments later is safe only through the idempotency keys. Doing it without them risks double charges.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: No change is proposed, so there is nothing to undo. If timeout or retry settings are changed later, revert them to their previous values.
